title: Methodology
content:
**Overall methodology.** The methodology is one harmonised observation chain, run from molecules to satellites along a single agricultural pressure gradient. The gradient runs from farmland, through the freshwater ecotones that receive its runoff, to the coastal waters downstream. One causal chain therefore carries the terrestrial, freshwater and marine realms the scope names. The central model is a multisensory integration architecture that reconciles molecular, plot, airborne and satellite observation under one protocol set. The method treats that reconciliation as an output to publish, not as internal scaffolding to discard.

**Concepts and assumptions.** Three assumptions underpin the design. A harmonisation decision taken for farmland can be verified in two downstream realms that did not design it. Observations from different measurement cultures become comparable only once one metadata standard binds them. A model validated on leaking data learns the site rather than the biology. These assumptions turn integration across the three realms from an assertion into a testable claim.

**How the methodology delivers the objectives.** The work is staged so each method rests on a finished one. A prioritised knowledge-gap and data-need analysis runs first and sets which gaps the three cases address. The joint protocols are agreed before any field campaign starts, because a case run under a protocol that later changes produces data the other cases cannot join. The three cases then run in sequence along the gradient, and each reuses the terrestrial protocol. The Cross-case verification report records which harmonisation decisions survived the transfer. European-scale mapping and trend prediction rest on the case models, so they come last.

**Methodological challenges and how we overcome them.** Reconciling four measurement cultures is the first challenge. The joint protocols and one metadata standard answer it. They bind the omics records to the in-situ and satellite records. The Genome-to-space linkage report is where that binding becomes a joinable record. The second challenge is harmonisation decisions failing to transfer between realms. The sequential case design exposes any failure in the Cross-case verification report rather than hiding it.

The third challenge is data leakage in model training. A leakage-safe split keeps site, season and treatment together in one fold. The fourth challenge is interoperability beyond the project boundary. Crosswalks to the European habitat classification (EUNIS) and the global ecosystem typology, publication to EOSC and the European Common Data Spaces, and contribution to the standards bodies carry the reconciliation outside the consortium. The fifth challenge is honest reporting at European scale. Trend predictions are delivered with stated uncertainty, so a map does not claim more confidence than the case models support.

**National and international R&I activities feeding the project.** The chain draws on external programmes and monitoring rather than rebuilding them. The satellite layer is built on the European earth-observation and navigation programmes, Copernicus and/or Galileo/EGNOS. The topic makes these an eligibility condition where satellite data are used. The terrestrial case ingests the Commission-steered monitoring data LUCAS grassland and EMBAL as a reference layer. The project earmarks effort for cooperation with GBIF, OBIS and LUCAS, and publishes its occurrence records to them. The training resource reworks a multi-season field archive of physiological, spectral, soil-water and weather measurements.

**Establishing those links.** Each link is carried by a defined task with an assigned owner, not by a letter of intent. A standing coordination interface runs to the FuturEO earth-observation projects in the same cluster. The project takes its harmonisation decisions to the standards bodies that maintain the European habitat classification and the global ecosystem typology. Published workflows and data are linked to EOSC and the European Common Data Spaces. Where a European research infrastructure offers a service the chain needs, the project uses it rather than rebuilding it. An open place in the project's interoperability work for the Joint Research Centre attaches to the crosswalk interface, and counts towards no eligibility condition.

**Interdisciplinary approach.** The approach is interdisciplinary by construction, because no single discipline spans molecules to satellites. It brings together molecular biology and genomics, in-situ ecology across farmland, freshwater and marine habitats, earth observation and geoinformatics, data engineering and artificial intelligence, and socio-ecological and policy analysis. The integration layer makes these disciplines interoperable. One protocol set, one metadata standard and the crosswalks bind a genomic observation and a satellite observation of the same place into one queryable record. Interdisciplinarity is therefore a method here, not a staffing table.

**Social sciences and humanities.** Social sciences and humanities are integral, because the pressure the project observes is socio-economic in origin. The scope asks for analysis of socio-economic pressures and for links to socio-ecological and climatic data, so these disciplines enter the research content. The integration architecture ingests socio-ecological and climatic data layers alongside the biophysical ones. Socio-economic driver analysis selects each demonstration case on pressure evidence rather than on data convenience. Policy and agricultural analysis then shapes the indicators to the reporting obligations and to farm-management decisions.

**Gender dimension in the research content.** The gender dimension applies to this topic, and the call binding compliance profile records a gender requirement. Sex and gender are not variables in the molecular, plot or satellite observation of ecosystems, so they are not analysed there. They are analysed where the research content involves people: the stakeholder engagement, the usability evaluation of the decision-support tools, and the farm-management uptake. There the project disaggregates practitioner and decision-maker participation and response by sex and gender. This keeps a tool from being validated on one group and deployed to another.

**Open science practices.** Open science is the project's core mechanism, not an add-on, because reuse is the stated ambition. The project delivers FAIR research data, harmonisation workflows and processing protocols, as the scope requires. It publishes datasets, workflows and services to EOSC and the European Common Data Spaces. Processing runs through provenance-tracked, reproducible pipelines, released openly, so a result can be replayed. Project occurrence records go to GBIF, OBIS and LUCAS, and the training and validation resource is published with its split protocol. Harmonisation decisions are contributed to the standards bodies, so the protocols and crosswalks outlive the project.

**Research data management.** A data management plan is delivered as a distinct deliverable within the first six months. The deliverable is the Data management plan and shared metadata profile. It makes research data findable, accessible, interoperable and reusable, and is updated as the data grow. It fixes the metadata standard the three cases share before the field campaigns open. The plan is therefore a condition of the integration, not a reporting formality.
